Assignment 8: Visualization - Making a bar race

Return Here: README

How to do it?:

  • Open the Rmarkdown file of this assignment (link) in Rstudio.

  • Right under each question, insert a code chunk (you can use the hotkey Ctrl + Alt + I to add a code chunk) and code the solution for the question.

  • Knit the rmarkdown file (hotkey: Ctrl + Alt + K) to export an html.

  • Publish the html file to your Githiub Page.

Submission: Submit the link on Github of the assignment to Canvas

  1. Install two packages gganimate and gifski then restart Rstudio. Using the Adult Census Income data, make an animation using geom_point and transition_states.
library("tidyverse")
## Warning: package 'tidyverse' was built under R version 4.5.3
## Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.5.3
## Warning: package 'readr' was built under R version 4.5.3
## Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.5.3
library("gganimate")
## Warning: package 'gganimate' was built under R version 4.5.3
library("gifski")
## Warning: package 'gifski' was built under R version 4.5.3
library("ggplot2")
df = read_csv("Data/adult_census.csv")
df %>% names
##  [1] "age"            "workclass"      "fnlwgt"         "education"     
##  [5] "education.num"  "marital.status" "occupation"     "relationship"  
##  [9] "race"           "sex"            "capital.gain"   "capital.loss"  
## [13] "hours.per.week" "native.country" "income"
# Its going to take all the points and translation them, its pretty cool
g = df %>% ggplot() + geom_point(mapping = aes(age, hours.per.week)) + transition_states(income)

animate(g)

  1. Using the Adult Census Income data, make an animation using geom_bar and transition_states.
# Going to just build a bars and then update the bars
g = df %>% ggplot() + geom_col(mapping = aes(sex, hours.per.week)) + transition_states(income)

animate(g)

  1. Use the WHO’s dataset at this link. Make a top-10 bar race by months between countries on the number of deaths by Covid 19 in 2021.
df = read_csv("Data/WHO-COVID-19-global-data.csv")
df %>% names
## [1] "Date_reported"     "Country_code"      "Country"          
## [4] "WHO_region"        "New_cases"         "Cumulative_cases" 
## [7] "New_deaths"        "Cumulative_deaths"
# First filter to 2021, then mutate to get month column
# Then group by month and country, then get the cumulative death counts
# Then group by month, and get your rank variable and then filter to top 10
d2 = df %>%
  filter(Date_reported > "2020-12-31" & Date_reported < "2022-01-01") %>%
  mutate(month = month(Date_reported)) %>%
  group_by(month, Country) %>%
  summarise(Cumulative_deaths = max(Cumulative_deaths, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  mutate(rank = rank(-Cumulative_deaths)) %>%
  filter(rank <= 10)


g = d2 %>% ggplot() +
  geom_col(mapping = aes(y = rank, x = Cumulative_deaths, fill = Country), orientation = "y") + scale_y_reverse() +
# need orientation = y for some reason to tell the bars to go left to right
  transition_states(month) +
  labs(x = "Rank",
       y = "Cumulative Deaths",
       title = "Month: {closest_state}")

animate(g)

  1. Make a bar race using a dataset of your own interest. You may use the dataset that we use in class (https://covidtracking.com/data/download/all-states-history.csv) but you should make a different bar racev from ones in the slides.
df = read_csv("Data/imdb_top_1000.csv")
# From AI its so I can get the genre to like 14 genres instead of so many
df$Main_Genre = str_extract(df$Genre, "^[^,]+")
df %>% names
##  [1] "Poster_Link"   "Series_Title"  "Released_Year" "Certificate"  
##  [5] "Runtime"       "Genre"         "IMDB_Rating"   "Overview"     
##  [9] "Meta_score"    "Director"      "Star1"         "Star2"        
## [13] "Star3"         "Star4"         "No_of_Votes"   "Gross"        
## [17] "Main_Genre"
# So 
d2 = df %>%
  # Parse number to get it into a number
  mutate(Released_Year = parse_number(Released_Year)) %>%
  filter(Released_Year >= 2000) %>%
  group_by(Released_Year, Main_Genre) %>%
  summarise(Gross = max(Gross, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  filter(Gross > 0) %>%
  group_by(Released_Year) %>%
  mutate(rank = rank(-Gross)) %>%
  filter(rank <= 10)
## Warning: There was 1 warning in `mutate()`.
## ℹ In argument: `Released_Year = parse_number(Released_Year)`.
## Caused by warning:
## ! 1 parsing failure.
## row col expected actual
## 967  -- a number     PG
## Warning: There were 8 warnings in `summarise()`.
## The first warning was:
## ℹ In argument: `Gross = max(Gross, na.rm = TRUE)`.
## ℹ In group 18: `Released_Year = 2002`, `Main_Genre = "Adventure"`.
## Caused by warning in `max()`:
## ! no non-missing arguments to max; returning -Inf
## ℹ Run `dplyr::last_dplyr_warnings()` to see the 7 remaining warnings.
g = d2 %>% ggplot() +
  geom_col(mapping = aes(y = rank, x = Gross, fill = Main_Genre), orientation = "y") +
  # to flip the ranking
  scale_y_reverse() +
  transition_states(Released_Year) +
  labs(x = "Gross",
       y = "Rank",
       title = "Year: {closest_state}")

animate(g)
